metaDesc: A real 3-day Koh Samui beach hopping plan covering buzzy Chaweng, laid-back Lamai, Bophut's fishing village, calm Choeng Mon, and Thong Takian (Silver Beach) where you can snorkel. With timings, routes, and real Thailand prices.

h1:
Koh Samui Beach Hopping Plan
Chaweng–Lamai–Bophut–Choeng Mon–Thong Takian
intro: Koh Samui packs a lot of different beaches into a small island, from the busy, crowded stretch of Chaweng to quiet little coves like Thong Takian where you can dip your face in the water and spot fish. This plan spreads five beaches across the east and north coasts over 3 days, with no rushing. Rent a scooter or grab a ride and you're set — including timings, routes, and the prices we actually saw in early 2026.

blocks.html: What makes Samui fun is that each beach has its own character. Chaweng is the island's hub for restaurants, bars, and crowds. Lamai is more relaxed but still has plenty to eat. Further north you hit Bophut, home to the Fisherman's Village and its walking street, then calm Choeng Mon, which suits families, and finally Thong Takian — also called Silver Beach — a small cove tucked between Lamai and Chaweng with the clearest water in the area. This plan covers all five without making you hurry.

blocks.title: Read this before you go
blocks.html: Samui's Gulf of Thailand water is clearest and calmest roughly from December to April. During the late-year monsoon (October–November) the water can turn murky with bigger waves. Before you swim or snorkel, always check the forecast and the warning flags at that particular beach.

blocks.text: The 5 beaches at a glance — pick your style

items.name: Chaweng Beach
items.blurb: A roughly 6 km stretch of white sand and the liveliest beach on the island, with restaurants, bars, shopping, and nightlife. The northern end is quieter and far less crowded.

items.name: Lamai Beach
items.blurb: Sand and water quality close to Chaweng but with a chiller, less crowded vibe — good for couples and families. The southern end has the Hin Ta and Hin Yai rock formations.

items.name: Bophut Beach
items.blurb: A breezy old-school beach with a fishing village and walking street, more about eating and strolling than swimming. It has a genuine local feel.

items.name: Choeng Mon Beach
items.blurb: Up in the northeast corner with calm, clear water that's easy to swim in — great for families with kids. There are resorts and beachfront cafes.

items.name: Thong Takian / Silver Beach
items.blurb: A small cove about 300 m long, hidden between Lamai and Chaweng, with the clearest water around here. Rocky outcrops on both sides and shallow coral mean you can spot fish just by looking down.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Chaweng + Thong Takian (main beach + hidden cove)

blocks.html: Start day one at Chaweng, which sits in the middle of the island. The water is clear and the crowds are thin in the morning, so it's easy to swim or walk the beach. In the afternoon, move down to Thong Takian (Silver Beach), just a few minutes south, then loop back to catch the nightlife at Chaweng.

items.note: Mornings mean cleaner sand, fewer people, and clearer water than the afternoon. The northern end of the beach is quieter than the middle.

items.activity: Break at a beachfront or side-street spot in Chaweng
items.note: There are loads of restaurants and cafes — everything from rice-and-curry shops to seafood. Prices vary by location.
It sits between Chaweng and Lamai. The entrance is a downhill lane — go carefully on a scooter on the steep bit. It's a small beach with limited parking.
There's coral and small fish like clownfish and angelfish near the rocks on both sides. The water is clearest from morning to early afternoon. Bring your own mask and watch out for sharp rocks.

items.activity: Back to Chaweng for sunset + a beach bar
items.note: Chaweng is the island's main nightlife zone, with Ark Bar and several beachfront bars. The music runs loud until late, so if you want a quiet night, pick a place away from the bar strip.

blocks.title: Honest talk about snorkeling on Samui
blocks.html: Most beaches on Koh Samui aren't crystal-clear snorkeling spots. Thong Takian is the best on this coast, but it's still shallow coral near the rocks. If you want to see real reefs and genuinely clear water, take a boat to Koh Tao or the Ang Thong Marine Park as a separate day trip. Always check the sea conditions and choose an operator that provides life jackets.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Lamai + Hin Ta Hin Yai

blocks.html: On day two, head south to Lamai, a beach that's more relaxed than Chaweng but still has plenty to eat and places to stay. The white sand and clear water are about on par with Chaweng, but it's less crowded and easy to stroll under the coconut palms. Then carry on to the Hin Ta and Hin Yai rocks at the southern end — a photo spot the whole island knows.

items.note: A chiller vibe than Chaweng, with shade from coconut palms. The water is clear in the dry season but can turn murky during the monsoon.

items.activity: Lunch at a Lamai beachfront spot
items.note: Several beachfront seafood and Thai restaurants, mid-range prices.

items.activity: Walk to Hin Ta Hin Yai
items.note: At the southern end of Lamai Beach. The oddly shaped rocks are one of the island's signature photo spots, with a walkway and souvenir shops nearby.
There are shops selling coconut desserts and sweets to try around here. Sit and rest before heading back.
Lamai has bars and laid-back spots for the evening without the noise of Chaweng — good for anyone who really wants to relax.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Bophut + Choeng Mon (north of the island)

blocks.html: On the last day, go north. Start at Bophut Beach and the Fisherman's Village — a district of old wooden houses with seaside eateries — then carry on to Choeng Mon in the northeast corner, where the calm, clear water is perfect for an easy swim and a relaxed end to the trip. If it falls on a Friday, the Bophut walking street runs in the evening for plenty of street food.

items.note: Old wooden houses by the sea, with cafes and restaurants lining the street. It's more about strolling, photos, and food than swimming.

items.activity: Seafood/brunch by the water in Bophut
items.note: Everything from grilled-prawn spots to modern cafes, with options for any budget.

Not far east of Bophut. The water is calm and clear, with soft sand in the middle of the beach that's good for swimming. Both ends are rocky, and even at low tide the middle stays deep enough to swim.
Great for families with kids, with resorts and beachfront cafes. Some resorts let outside guests sit in if you order something.

The Fisherman's Village walking street runs every Friday, roughly 17:00–22:00 (sometimes until 23:00). Lots of food, big crowds, limited parking — come by scooter or grab a ride, and arrive before 18:30 for an easier walk.

blocks.html: All five beaches are on the east and north coasts and aren't far apart — Chaweng to Lamai or Bophut is about 15 minutes. The most flexible way to get around is renting a scooter, but some roads are steep and the entrance to small beaches like Thong Takian is a downhill slope. Ride slowly and always wear a helmet.

items: Scooter rental — around ฿150–300 per day, the most flexible option, but you need a license and should watch out for steep roads and slippery rain.
Songthaew (shared truck) — around ฿60–100 per person depending on distance, running along the main routes — fine if you're not in a hurry.
Taxi/private hire — around ฿150–600 per trip between the main beaches depending on distance; agree on the fare before you get in.
Grab — available in the main tourist zones, easy to book but with fewer cars than in a big city.

blocks.title: Careful on a scooter here
blocks.html: Samui's roads include steep climbs, sharp bends, and spots where traffic moves fast. If you're not used to riding a scooter, take a songthaew or private car instead. Always wear a helmet, avoid riding in the rain when roads get slippery, and check the bike and brakes before you take it every time.

blocks.text: Which beach should you stay at?

blocks.html: If you want to do all five beaches conveniently, staying around Chaweng or Bophut puts you in the middle with easy access. Chaweng suits people who like buzz and nightlife. Lamai suits anyone who wants it quieter but still has food nearby. Bophut suits people who like the village atmosphere and seaside eateries, while Choeng Mon suits families who want calm water and quiet.

faq.q: How many days do you need to see Koh Samui's beaches?
faq.a: To cover Chaweng, Lamai, Bophut, Choeng Mon, and Thong Takian without rushing, about 3 days is just right, since the beaches are on the east and north coasts and aren't far apart — Chaweng to Lamai or Bophut is roughly 15 minutes. If you only have 1 day, do Chaweng in the morning and Thong Takian in the afternoon, then finish with the nightlife at Chaweng to get the gist.

faq.q: Which Samui beach has the clearest water and best snorkeling?
faq.a: On the east coast, Thong Takian (Silver Beach) has the clearest water, with shallow coral and small fish near the rocks, making it better for snorkeling than the other beaches. But most beaches on Koh Samui aren't crystal clear, so if you want to see real reefs, take a boat to Koh Tao or the Ang Thong Marine Park as a separate day trip.

faq.q: Which beach is best for kids and families?
faq.a: Choeng Mon in the northeast corner has calm, clear water with few waves and is easy to swim in — the best for bringing kids. Next is Lamai, which is relaxed and has shade. Chaweng is crowded and has a nightlife zone, which can be hectic for families who want quiet.

faq.q: What day is the Bophut walking street open?
faq.a: The walking street at the Bophut Fisherman's Village runs every Friday, roughly 17:00–22:00, sometimes until 23:00. There's lots of food, big crowds, and limited parking, so come by scooter or grab a ride, and arrive before 18:30 for an easier walk.

faq.q: What's the best way to travel between beaches on Samui?
faq.a: A scooter is the most flexible, around ฿150–300 per day, but you need a license and should watch for steep roads and slippery rain. If you're not used to riding, take a songthaew (around ฿60–100 per person) or hire a taxi (around ฿150–600 per trip). Always agree on the fare before you get in.
